# ANTIMICROBIAL PROPHYLAXIS AND DERMATOLOGIC SURGERY

**St. Cloud Guidance (Inpatient):**

RECOMMENDATIONS NOT AVAILABLE
Recommendations for this condition are not available within CDSS. Please refer to facility guidelines or other clinical resources for recommendations.

**Minneapolis Guidance:**

Antibiotics are used to prevent infections in patients undergoing surgery in certain well-defined circumstances. They are used to prevent surgical site infection or to prevent endocarditis in circumstances where the risk of endocarditis is high. For many low-risk surgeries, the risks associated with antibiotic use, which can be severe or cause death, outweigh the benefits. The following recommendations are consistent with guidelines published by the American Heart Association and Infectious Disease Society of America.

In general, antibiotics are used to prevent post-operative wound infection in clean-contaminated surgery. Most dermatological surgery involves clean sites, and the risks of antibiotics outweigh potential benefits. Antibiotics are used to prevent endocarditis and hematogenous joint infection in procedures involving infected skin structures. Antibitic prophylaxis is also recommended to prevent surgical site infections in procedures involving high risk surgical sites and conditions.

When they are used, prophylactic oral antimicrobial agents should be administered 30-60 minutes before the first tissue manipulation or incision.

Intravenous antimicrobials should be administered 60 minutes (120 minutes for vancomycin) prior to procedure.

Antimicrobials should not be used to prevent infections in patients with vascular grafts or orthopedic prostheses because the risk of bacteremia or infection of these devices is tiny and antibiotic risks outweigh any theoretical benefit.

A full course of antibiotics should be used to treat skin infections where infection is already present at the time of surgery.

Suggested antibiotic prophylaxis regimens should be targeted against the typical pathogens likely to be present. A risk-based approach for coverage of MRSA should be taken in patients with specific risk factors for MRSA.
